tagline.text: National shrine on the birthplace of reformer Plaridel in Bulacan

location.label: Location
location.text: Sitio Cupang, Barangay San Nicolas, Bulakan, Bulacan

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100~300 (including transport, per person for a day trip)

children.text: Marcelo H. del Pilar was a reformist who led the newspaper La Solidaridad during the Spanish colonial era, writing under the pen name Plaridel. A national shrine now stands on his family's former home site in Sitio Cupang, Bulakan, where you can see his monument, tomb and a museum in one stop.

The Marcelo H. del Pilar Shrine is a national shrine in Sitio Cupang, Barangay San Nicolas, in Bulakan, Bulacan. Marcelo del Pilar was born on August 30, 1850, in the family house that once stood on this very spot. Better known by his pen name "Plaridel," he is counted with José Rizal among the leaders of the reform (Propaganda) movement in the Spanish colonial period. The shrine is owned by the Philippine government and managed by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP).
The site covers about

, and at its center stands a monument about 10 feet (about 3 m) tall by sculptor Apolinario Bulaong. The statue is made of cement mixed with crushed bronze, and del Pilar's remains rest beneath it. He died of tuberculosis in Barcelona, Spain, on July 4, 1896; his remains were returned to Manila in 1920 and placed in the Manila North Cemetery, then moved to his birthplace on August 30, 1984. In other words, this is both his birthplace and his burial place.

Knowing a little of his life makes the shrine much more vivid. He was baptized on September 4, 1850, a few days after his birth, at the Our Lady of the Assumption Church in Bulakan. He later worked as a lawyer and journalist, criticizing abuses by the colonial government and the religious orders, and in Spain he led the newspaper La Solidaridad and called for reform in the Philippines. His health failed, and he died around 1:15 a.m. on July 4, 1896, at the Hospital de la Santa Cruz in Barcelona. He was buried the next day in a borrowed grave at Montjuïc Cemetery in Barcelona, moved in December 1920 to the Mausoleum of the Veterans of the Revolution in the Manila North Cemetery, and finally returned to his home ground in 1984. That his remains, after roughly 90 years of wandering, now lie where he was born is the shrine's central story.

Behind the monument stands the family mausoleum. It is said to hold a family tree of del Pilar's descendants and the remains of his wife Marciana and other relatives. Deeper in the grounds is a two-storey museum-library that opened in 1998. Built in the style of a traditional Filipino bahay na bato house, it displays del Pilar's writings and books about Filipino heroes, with a library and gallery on the second floor. The shrine took a long time to take shape. A historical marker was first placed in 1939, groundbreaking is said to have been held on August 30, 1956, and the site turned over in 1983 to the National Historical Institute (the predecessor of the NHCP), per Wikipedia. It was declared a national shrine by a board resolution in 2006, and a revised historical marker was installed on January 17, 2012. It is not a large attraction, but it is a quiet place to reflect on a moment in modern Philippine history. Its closeness to Manila is another plus: the town of Bulakan lies about
35km

north of Manila. Bulakan was the former capital of Bulacan and still has a church, birthplace sites and heroes' monuments, so the shrine fits well into a Bulacan history trip that includes Malolos Cathedral and Barasoain Church.

At the center of the grounds stands a monument about 10 feet tall. It is the work of sculptor Apolinario Bulaong, and because del Pilar's remains rest beneath it, it serves as both statue and tomb. Many visitors pause for a quiet moment of respect and take photos.

This is where the del Pilar family house stood, and he was born here on August 30, 1850. The present structures are not the original house but were built as a memorial, so it is best to treat the visit as seeing the meaning of the site.
The mausoleum behind the monument is said to hold a family tree of descendants and the remains of his wife Marciana and other family members. It lets you see the story of a family, not just one man.

This two-storey building was built in 1998 and its exterior imitates the bahay na bato style. It displays del Pilar's writings and books about heroes, with a library and gallery on the second floor. Exhibits may change, so check on site.

blocks.title: La Solidaridad and the reform movement

children.text: Del Pilar led the newspaper La Solidaridad in Spain and brought the problems of colonial rule to public attention. The displays and signs give a clear picture of how Philippine national awareness grew.

A marker first placed in 1939 stands here, and a revised marker was installed on January 17, 2012. The text summarizes the main events of his life, which also makes it a good English reading exercise.

blocks.title: Tidy grounds and a calm atmosphere

children.text: With wide lawns and shade trees, the site is quiet compared with crowded attractions. You can rest in the shade even on a hot day and take your time, and it is a good place to tell children about history.

blocks.title: The journey home of his remains

children.text: Follow the route of his remains from Montjuïc Cemetery in Barcelona through the Manila North Cemetery to the site of his birth. Thinking about the long time until his burial here on August 30, 1984, changes what you feel in front of the monument.

items.title: Half-day course
items.subtitle: The shrine and a walk through Bulakan town

children.text: Leave Manila and head toward Malolos or Balagtas. Allow about
1.5–2.5 hours
depending on traffic.
Take a tricycle from Bulakan town to the shrine. It takes within about
10–15 minutes
from the town center; check the fare locally.
Pay your respects before the monument and tomb and read the markers. Look around the family mausoleum as well.
See the exhibits in the museum-library building. You need to arrive within opening hours, so coming in the morning is safer.
Return to Bulakan town for lunch and look around the Bulakan church and the nearby heroes' monuments.
Opening hours and closing days differ by source, so ask the NHCP before you leave or check the latest announcements.
See del Pilar's life story and the exhibits at the shrine.
Walk around the Bulakan church and the town's heritage sites.
Move on to Malolos for lunch.
Visit Malolos Cathedral and Barasoain Church to follow on the background of the era in which del Pilar was active.
Visiting several sites by public transport takes time, so a UV van or a car with a driver is more convenient.
The usual way is to take a bus or UV van toward Malolos or Bulakan. Departure points and routes change often, so check the latest information.
Jeepneys are said to run to Bulakan from Malolos, Balagtas and Obando. There is a tricycle terminal in front of Bulakan Church.
From town to the shrine is a short tricycle ride. Local drivers often call it "Marcelo," so say the name clearly.
Travel time varies greatly with traffic. Avoid weekends and rush hours.
It is about
35km
north of Manila. Search for "Marcelo H. del Pilar Shrine" on Google Maps.
Check locally whether parking is available at the shrine entrance.
A one-way tricycle ride from near Bulakan Church to the shrine is reported to cost about
(from one travel wiki, 2026; tricycle fares start at ₱30; check locally).
The town is small, so a tricycle is usually enough.
The dry season from November to May is comfortable for walking the outdoor grounds. December to February is relatively cool and especially pleasant for walking.

During the rainy season from June to November, expect showers and possible road flooding. Del Pilar's birthday, August 30, falls in the rainy season but is a meaningful day, so check NHCP announcements for any commemorations.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.
There are few large lodgings near the shrine. You can make a day trip from Manila, or, to stay overnight, Malolos city center offers more choices.

It is easier to eat in Bulakan town or Malolos. The Bulakan area is close to rivers, and fish and shrimp dishes are said to be common, so ask local restaurants for the day's recommendation. We suggest bringing your own snacks and water.

Restaurants in Bulakan town can get crowded at weekend lunchtime, so we recommend seeing the shrine in the morning and reaching your lunch spot around 12:00. Traffic back to Manila is heavy in the evening, so it is best to leave before 4 p.m.
Ask the NHCP about opening hours before you go. Hours and closing days differ by source.
Going in the morning avoids the heat and keeps you from missing the museum's hours.
Tell the tricycle driver "Marcelo H. del Pilar Shrine" or "Marcelo" and he will understand.
There is a separate monument to his nephew Gregorio del Pilar nearby, so do not confuse the two.
Because it is a burial place, keep your voice down and dress modestly.
Follow the on-site instructions on photography rules.
Bring water, a hat and sunscreen.
It is efficient to combine the visit with Bulakan Church.
Our Lady of the Assumption Church (Bulakan Church) is where del Pilar was baptized, so visiting it on the same day continues the story.
If the history is unfamiliar, read a short introduction to del Pilar, La Solidaridad and the Propaganda movement before you go; the exhibits will make much more sense.
Hours and closing days differ by source, so you could make a wasted trip; be sure to confirm before visiting.
There are reports that it is closed on Mondays and holidays, so avoid those days.
Roads can flood in the rainy season, so check the weather.
Public transport routes and fares change, so recheck locally.
Watch your belongings and avoid visiting late in the day.
Bulakan town near the shrine has a church and heroes' monuments close together. It is about
10–15 minutes
away by tricycle.
It is known as one of the places where del Pilar carried out his anti-friar activities. It is about
30 minutes
from the shrine by car, depending on traffic.
This is where the First Philippine Republic's congress met in 1898. It is in Malolos city, so it is easy to combine on the same day.
A pilgrimage site south of Bulacan that you can add to your itinerary if the timing fits.
